story_text.value:
I built Klistra: describe your video idea and add your logo, photos or other assets, Klistra designs and animates a video for you, exported for every screen size, with fonts, media and logos kept exact. Deterministic renders make features exact and isolated, allowing for superior control and iteration compared to diffusion models. Here's a short demo render where I made an ad for Klistra itself: https://app.klistra.ai/s/4EQoWCe37SkYz5nThgegzw

As a solo dev with a lot of projects going on, I found myself needing to make short promos or explainer videos. Not being familiar with animation software, I had the idea to use Claude to code up those videos and export them as video files. In the process of creating these clips I stumbled into a bunch of bugs and setup needed to make it work reliably. The list of features I wanted for better control and feedback kept growing and I needed to sign up for a bunch of services to get music, voiceovers and other media into my project. I couldn't find an existing service that had everything I wanted. Seeing these hurdles and that the technology was only easily accessible to people already confident with coding agents, I started working on Klistra, and a couple of months later I'm turning it into a service so you all can use it too.

The goal with Klistra was to include everything I missed in the manual workflow in an easy-to-use service with a nice UI, so people could focus on what they wanted the video to look like, not setting up the framework behind it. Klistra includes precise timeline control, media generation, built-in support to make animations match the rhythm of the background music, word extraction from voiceovers or songs, a dedicated iteration / feedback tool, website import and much more.

Something I knew I needed to get right was making it easy to iterate on small features of the video with precise control of what was being built. I designed Klistra so you first create a specification where you define scenes in detail, describe what you want shown and when, reference media or timestamps in-line, freely drag the timeline around and preview the result before letting a builder agent create the video. If you want to change something, the specification changes and the builder agent gets a diff of what changed. There is also a planner agent built into Klistra that helps create and edit the specification for you (which is what I use the most), while letting you turn to manual fine-tuning when needed.

Don't think of this as a replacement for diffusion models, if you want photorealistic images or videos they clearly do a better job. Klistra really shines when you need motion design and precise control, exact text with your fonts, media such as logos or voiceovers, animated UI that matches your apps and so on. Klistra does have built-in integrations for generating media from diffusion models, and combining the two technologies usually gets the best results.

Everything that costs money to run on Klistra, from machines to AI tokens, is paid for with credits included in a subscription or bought via one-time packs (Pro starts at $25/mo ($20 billed yearly) and packs at $12). Being a solo dev without funding, the budget wouldn't allow for a free tier with enough monthly credits for a real project. I instead decided to give the first 200 of you who sign up 350 free credits, enough for a simple video (the advanced tutorial used around 250 credits).

There is also a Claude Code integration in paid subscriptions, where your agent can act as a planner, convenient if you already have a project built with Claude that has all the context and you need an explainer, ad or social post. It also reduces credit spending if you're a heavy planner user.

- Tutorial, mostly using the planner: https://klistra.ai/docs/basic

- Advanced features and manual control: https://klistra.ai/docs/advanced

- More demos: https://klistra.ai/

Happy to hear what you think!

story_text.value:
I’m writing my first novel and could not find an app that fit my workflow: quiet like iA Writer, organized like Scrivener, and with AI so I can discuss my book while I write it. It allows me to feel less “alone” and have a sounding board while I write.

- A book is a folder of plain Markdown files. Musset commits to a git repo, tracks versions and drafts without you having to know git.

- Revisions are CriticMarkup inside the text. It manages docx revisions too, so your editor can edit a Word doc and you import their comments.

- PDFs are typeset using Typst, embedded in the app, following each language’s typographic rules.

- Spelling and grammar are checked using LanguageTool, also embedded.

- Mac/Word, WordStar, vi and Emacs keyboard modes.

The AI is optional and uses your Codex or Claude Code CLI. It comments, leaves margin notes, and checks continuity and your chapters against your style rules.

It’s GPL-3.0 and free during the beta. When or if it reaches 1.0, if there is sufficient interest, the idea is to make it a small one-time payment ($9.90). There is a paid sync service (git hosting) that lets you share a book with beta readers and editors.

Download: https://musset.app

I’d love to have some feedback!

story_text.value:
Hi Hackernews! I just wanted to share a game I've made over a few weeks just as a little side project. Of course it was developed using Agents Engineering. The idea of the game though comes from around 10 years ago, from conversations with my brother: he is an artist and back them he was experimenting with chromatic paintings that looked differently depending on which color of light they were exposed to. A few weeks ago I decided to show my brother what's possible now a days with AI and how we can turn ideas into reality with a fraction of the effort we would have need in the past. The game is a little platformer, meant to be challenging but cute and entertaining, taking inspiration of games like Celeste or Meatboy. Death is part of the game, and light mechanics are introduced over the course of the 63 levels that are available to play.

The development was made fully from my phone with Claude Code, but I invested lots of time on play testing it and I've involved several friends to play it to gather feedback and improve it.

I'd love to hear your feedback and I hope some of you have fun playing it!

title.value: Show HN: Trichroma, a Platformer of Light

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Bryant, founder of ArkViz (https://arkviz.io). ArkViz is a product to automatically generate architecture diagrams from your codebase using AI.

The vision behind ArkViz is to supercharge both AI agents and humans by providing AI agents deeper relational context using structured model diagram formats, and by providing humans with a rich visual representation you can interact with, with features like zooming, panning, search, and show composing files.

In this new age of AI, you can generate a structured model diagram from your codebase in seconds, quicker and better than a human. Not only can the generated diagram be a visual documentation tool for humans, AI agents can also benefit from the context of a pre-generated architecture diagram that lives alongside a project’s codebase. This concept has already been proven by context files like CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md living in the root of your repository.

The differentiator between ARCHITECTURE.md and ArkViz is that ArkViz generates a structured model diagram of the system, while ARCHITECTURE.md is broader in scope and purely text. ArkViz aims to be a supplement to ARCHITECTURE.md to provide deeper understanding like how components are connected, which components live inside other components, which files compose a component.

—

Why ArkViz?

Software engineering teams often create diagrams to aid in the documentation of their software systems. They are incredibly useful for onboarding new engineers and understanding projects. However, they take time to create and maintain, so are often non-existent or out of date. ArkViz automates the creation and maintenance of software architecture diagrams, seamlessly and securely.

AI agents thrive when they have high quality context, including for architecture diagrams. However not all diagram formats out there are optimized for AI. A diagram showing connected systems and components can be represented in essentially 3 ways:

1. Unstructured drawing / canvas format (e.g. draw.io, Excalidraw, Figma, LucidChart)

  - Quick to get started but hard to maintain.
  - Good for brainstorming and whiteboarding
  - The format carries no semantic meaning and is basically represented by pixels, shapes, and vectors. Positioning is stored
  - Passing this to an AI agent as context has questionable value.
2. Structured diagramming formats (e.g. Mermaid, d2lang)

  - A level of abstraction higher than a 2D drawing canvas
  - Good for quick isolated diagram, like on GitHub
  - Represented by nodes and edges, nested hierarchies. Layout is generated
  - Better for AI agents, although they have to piece together the context, and might get confused by an inconsistency like duplicate naming
3. Structured modeling formats (e.g. Structurizr, LikeC4, IcePanel).

  - These have an underlying data model and single source of truth
  - High quality documentation, but hard to create and maintain
  - Represented by entities and relationships. Layout can be richer, like zooming into a component and seeing what's inside
  - Best for AI agents, since they have a single source of truth context
ArkViz currently uses LikeC4 for its diagram format, a modern, popular, and open-source architecture-as-code format that supports interactive diagrams. AI agents will be more trained with this than a proprietary format.

Why not roll my own solution with something like Claude Code? While Claude Code is a powerful AI coding harness, ArkViz provides seamless features you'd rather not spend time building like hosting diagrams, access control, scheduling automation, handling errors and retries, logs, connectors to GitHub. Additionally, ArkViz has battle-tested, optimized multi-pass prompts, validators, and guardrails for the specific purpose of AI generated architecture diagrams.

Take a look here: https://arkviz.io! Feedback greatly appreciated on which features you care about, and whether you think the value proposition is there.

story_text.value:
Hello!

One of my hobbies is curling in a league with the local curling club. From time to time, there's a setup of stones that is tricky and interesting to contemplate from a strategic perspective. A while back, I started working on a three.js-based curling simulator that would enable me to recreate situations from my league games and then try different shots.

As you may know, curling is notoriously tricky from a physics perspective. There are a variety of papers out there about this, including this one, which is one of the more recent dives into understanding why stones curl the way they do: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-26595-y

Anyhow, with the help of Claude Code, I pulled together the work and converted the quick-and-dirty sim into a game you can play online. It's still a bit more of a sim than a game, perhaps, but it can be fun to play as a game.

Curling often is referred to as "chess on ice" because there's more strategy in choosing shots and playing ends than there would appear to be at first glance. The primary challenge of turning this into a game has been trying to figure out how to provide the computer player both with a policy for game and end-level strategy while also having it evaluate the tactical choices that have to be made for each shot.

For example, when would the computer try to blank (no points scored) an end deliberately so that it can retain hammer (last stone thrown) in the subsequent end? When should it throw a low vs. high center or corner guard in an attempt to make up a point deficit? When should it try to steal points from the hammer team vs. throwing protective stones that hold the hammer team to one point?

It's a fun side project for me, so I thought you all might enjoy giving it a shot. :)

p.s. In a game, if you go into the settings, you can turn on debug mode, which will reveal a panel on the right with a variety of (currently-undocumented) parameters you can tweak.

story_text.value:
Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning!

You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YlkIc3L29lo

A (somewhat long) summary:

When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways.

Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio.

Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said.

The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. With a single LLM in the pipeline, the obvious choice is picking one fast enough to feel responsive, but that comes with an unavoidably high error rate on real calls, frustrating callers and sending calls off the rails.

More recently, end-to-end “speech-to-speech” models have won usage alongside three-step pipelines. They’re better at hearing callers correctly (though still not perfect), but they’re even worse at following instructions reliably, which is typically disastrous for business phone calls.

Once we understood these problems, we built our own stack to address them. Over the past year and a half, the ThunderPhone stack has largely solved mishearing and misbehaving by combining numerous models on each call.

For audio misunderstandings, we run multiple, even numerous, transcription models on most calls, giving more “shots on goal” from the original audio. Even if none gets it exactly right, multiple almost-correct answers let us triangulate on a correct transcript, using one or more LLMs to decide what the caller actually said. In challenging situations, we even pipe caller audio directly to one or more audio-input LLMs to further improve comprehension.

For instruction following, we run a mix of fast and slow LLMs on conversation turns to combine snappy responses with deeper thinking behind the scenes. In practice, this is a multi-staged classification problem: after 50ms, 500ms, 1s, etc., we simultaneously generate responses with increasing inference while classifying whether we need to “think harder” to generate a definitive correct answer.

Together with other smaller optimizations, these two approaches have been very effective. Qualitatively, customer calls go much more smoothly and reach successful outcomes far more frequently than on three-step or speech-to-speech pipelines. Quantitatively, we’ve set a record of 99.4% on the Big Bench Audio benchmark, smarter than any other model fast enough for real calls. (We’re also benchmarking ThunderPhone on more public benchmarks - stay tuned.)

The downside is configuration complexity. Every agent benefits from a different setup on the ThunderPhone stack, and even individual call turns on the same call often benefit from different stacks. Configuring this manually worked for enterprise customers, but made it prohibitive to give smaller self-serve customers the full benefits without giving their agents our full attention.

That’s how Zeus came about. Our enterprise configurations were repetitive enough that an AI could do them once we taught it how and gave it the right tools. We’re big fans of Claude Code and Codex for software development, but they fall short at configuring voice agents for a few reasons.

First, unlike software development, where you can compile code and run tests to verify things work, you can’t run live calls inside a computer right after configuring a voice agent - and coding agents don’t know how to run simulated calls out of the box, or “listen” to a call to spot real problems. We built both capabilities into Zeus, giving it a “closed loop” experience building, testing, and improving voice agents just like coding agents have with regular software.

Second, coding agents are pretty gullible about marketing claims. Companies building AI and voice infrastructure commonly post the most favorable possible interpretation of their capabilities online. Claude and Codex read those claims, believe them uncritically, and pick tools based on marketing rather than real performance. At best, that leads to suboptimal architectural choices; at worst, to voice agents that don’t really work at all.

We’ve sidestepped this with continuous evals feeding an internal knowledge base. For everything that matters for voice agents - accurate audio understanding, instruction following, noise cancelling, turn-taking, and more - we maintain internal benchmarks built on real call data. Every time a new AI model comes out, we (now mostly automatically) feed it through our evals for performance, speed, cost, and reliability/consistency. That feeds our internal knowledge base, which Zeus uses to pick the right stack for every agent, call, and conversation turn.

This all happens behind the scenes to keep the ThunderPhone experience seamless. A user just describes their use case and goals, and Zeus helps fill in ambiguities, connect VoIP and software integrations, and optimize the voice agent(s) on simulated and live calls until they hit the highest performance on business goals (conversions, unit economics, etc.) possible with today’s models.

Zeus is also differentiated on cost. Zeus itself is free to use for now, though we expect to move to subscription or token-based pricing later. For calls, we’ve become the first voice AI vendor to our knowledge to charge on a cost-plus basis: ThunderPhone customers pay exactly what we pay our vendors, plus a 17% margin on calls costing 2c/min or less, scaling linearly up to 25% for calls costing us 15c/min or more, and 25% from there on up.

However, we find that simple phone agents do well on a stack that costs about 2c/min, and more complex cases typically land around 5-10c/min - significantly cheaper than most alternatives.

Zeus is brand-new, so we’re eager to get feedback on how it works for customers, and any areas we could improve it. Give it a try and see what you think - let me know if you have any feedback or questions.

Alex

Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning!

You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YlkIc3L29lo

A (somewhat long) summary:

When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways.

Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio.

Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said.

The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. With a single LLM in the pipeline, the obvious choice is picking one fast enough to feel responsive, but that comes with an unavoidably high error rate on real calls, frustrating callers and sending calls off the rails.

More recently, end-to-end “speech-to-speech” models have won usage alongside three-step pipelines. They’re better at hearing callers correctly (though still not perfect), but they’re even worse at following instructions reliably, which is typically disastrous for business phone calls.

Once we understood these problems, we built our own stack to address them. Over the past year and a half, the ThunderPhone stack has largely solved mishearing and misbehaving by combining numerous models on each call.

For audio misunderstandings, we run multiple, even numerous, transcription models on most calls, giving more “shots on goal” from the original audio. Even if none gets it exactly right, multiple almost-correct answers let us triangulate on a correct transcript, using one or more LLMs to decide what the caller actually said. In challenging situations, we even pipe caller audio directly to one or more audio-input LLMs to further improve comprehension.

For instruction following, we run a mix of fast and slow LLMs on conversation turns to combine snappy responses with deeper thinking behind the scenes. In practice, this is a multi-staged classification problem: after 50ms, 500ms, 1s, etc., we simultaneously generate responses with increasing inference while classifying whether we need to “think harder” to generate a definitive correct answer.

Together with other smaller optimizations, these two approaches have been very effective. Qualitatively, customer calls go much more smoothly and reach successful outcomes far more frequently than on three-step or speech-to-speech pipelines. Quantitatively, we’ve set a record of 99.4% on the Big Bench Audio benchmark, smarter than any other model fast enough for real calls. accessible with vim keybinds, of course.

story_text.value:
I look up a lot at the sky at night and made this because I wanted to better understand what is up there.

Orbital shows all 32,000+ tracked objects at their current positions: about 17,000 working satellites, 2,800 dead ones, 2,200 spent rocket bodies and 10,700 pieces of debris.

Each is color coded, can be switched off, and can be "clicked" to follow. For the well-known ones it pulls up a real photo (where available), what it is for, and when it stopped working.

There is an animation that shows launch history from 1957 to today. When you first visit, click on the "Watch 1957 → today" button to see the animation.

You can also "fly out" to the solar system and see the planets, moons, comets and spacecraft further out there.

My orbit data comes from Space-Track. I also pull from CelesTrak to determine which satellites are currently active.

It is a static site on GitHub Pages (currently) with no backend, no accounts, and no ads. It also installs as an app and reopens offline.

I wrote it with Claude Code doing most of the implementation. I will provide the link to the source if you want it.

I would like to hear what you think about it. Specifically, what is confusing on a first visit, and what would make you come back to it. And anything else constructive you would like to share.

story_text.value:
This open-source TUI and CLI allows running the workflows that android devs run every day without leaving the terminal and each one in their own worktree.

You can see the agents working in a control pane with different status. The TUI will inform you when it needs your help.

You can: 1. Create a Pull Request from a ticket, the harness does a plan -> code -> review workflow. You can decide the model per state. 2. Auto fix the ticket comments, the harness fetches the PR comments and show it in the dashboard. You can previsualize and approve or request a new fix. 3. Review the diff, the TUI has a beauty diff viewer so you can review the code without leaving the terminal. 4. Open the worktree in Android Studio or claude code directly from the TUI. 5. Permission and budget management: you can auto approve comments or approve once. You can also set a spend limit per stage.

It is optimized for android: 1. Only one agent at a time can take control of the emulator. 2. The worktree creation, all git operations and PR information is deterministic and handled by the harness taking into consideration how Android projects are built. 3. Open the worktree in Android Studio. 4. Open the emulator from the TUI.

Caveats: For now it only works for Claude Code.

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook (https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com).

Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community.

Here’s a demo video: (https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM)

If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild.

We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do.

More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state).

Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862, August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449, May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code.

How it works…

Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal.

When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas.

The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant.

Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is.

This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt.

We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built.

The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams.

We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code!

The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day!
